I really really want to give this a "mixed" but feel the need to give it NR since I can't straight-up recommend it (had a few untracked hours of several 1CCs). I know the devs really want their high % and *probably* deserve it but I hope this review won't really dent it. Does that make sense? For me, it's an "okay" game. But I don't feel it has the staying power.

Anyway, the short of it is that I think I just don't "get" this game. Maybe it's a me thing, maybe it's the fact that I don't really fw CAVE shmups that much, but even after a few hours of just doing runs and clearing the game, nothing has ever "clicked" with me about it the way most other shmups have. My hunch is that this game is very much scoring-based and tailors to those who can squeeze the score out of the system as the main goal, but maybe I just don't vibe with the way sub weapons work here. They are VERY powerful at times and other times just another option (again, maybe more for scoring).

More importantly, I don't find the gameplay too memorable. In fact, I'd say that even on Parallel, this game feels more of a euroshmup in the way of lots of aimed bullets and fat mooks that don't die instantly but still darn pretty fast to the point there seems to be plenty of downtime that keeps ebbing and flowing in and back again. I haven't timed it or anything - I think the game is short for one session, but it doesn't FEEL short to me. Given what I've seen people say about it being more akin to DDP, you supposedly have to actively memorize the stages to get mileage out of it? But I'm sort of operating on pure instinct each time because I sort of don't remember what I'm doing and (to its credit) the shottypes play pretty differently. That said, I can really only remember the theme of each level and not what its quirks are (there's the one stage that has a % filling up for some reason, you get to fight Val who's one pattern is moving from side to side that I remember mostly because of how she's small and you have to catch her, the big stage 4 boss is cool ig). I really do feel like most of the dodging and the way to take down enemies is very much the same no matter where you are at in the game. It's not that it's a particularly difficult game, either. Parallel was very much comfortable to me, and I'm not afraid to lay waste with bombs. But that's why at times it felt cheesable which can either be satisfying or gives a hollow feeling.

Additionally, I don't find the game very beautiful. The rotsprites and thick chunky spritework are a bit unique but really don't do it for me given how the sprites and backgrounds are paletted because I think there's much variation in the designs of enemies. It kind of all turns into mush especially with the default colors (filters don't really do it for me) and I believe visibility is a problem with the default settings. Having to turn the background way down is a crime and so is turning the player shots and score points down, but it's the only way to fully see what's going on. I really like how the BGs seem almost painterly and abstract but I just can't do it as-is.

Music is okay. I don't really know if I should comment on it much, it's very much electronic, I suppose. It's a plus that there's a big variety of it and you can unlock more variations of them to your choosing, but the one I really like the most is the Stage 2 one which leads me to believe that every water-themed shmup stage has the best song. However, sound design is a bit of a letdown. For a while I wasn't even sure if there was a sfx for the player shooting and don't know if there's one for when damage has been done to an enemy. Explosions sound muddy and eh. There's just a lot of actions in-game that could have more auditory feedback but lack them. 

That's about it for my thoughts, which are a bit more than I thought I'd write about. It's probably rambly. I thought maybe XP-Mode would tickle my fancy but it's not really a real mode since you can only do it in Stage Select for one stage and I *still* didn't "get it" either. In a way there is definitely a lot of labour of love to be had in this game if they straight-up added what's effectively a 2.0 with more music and an overhaul, but it just really doesn't do it for me. Maybe I'll try the original arrangement sometime but doubt I'll feel any different. It's just that this game seems very popular, though I feel it's just in spite of how it's fending for itself as an indie shmup (niche genre). That's why I can't say Blue Revolver stands out to me as a game I'd egg people to play. Maybe get it on sale if you'd like what this game is trying to replicate and then you can up the score on my behalf.

Also, I don't fw the twitter-ahh blazblue character designs. Wish story was more in-the-way.

Relative shmup beginner. This is a quality shmup, which tends towards faster bullet patterns that aren't overly complex or layered and which has a strong focus on resource management, with both bombs and a special attack meter to manage - the bombs feed into the special meter and have a timing element since bullets convert to meter items, so there's a nice amount of depth here. The special also makes the enemy drop score items, and accruing score to certain points gives you an extra 1UP, and there's an additional system where you break parts of special enemies & certain boss phases in order to gain extra score. I like the mechanics, though I didn't actually engage with the break system much and it's one of those mechanics that doesn't make itself obvious in the game. (Which is not exactly uncommon - there are some very oblique scoring mechanics in shmups.)

The biggest issue I have - playing on Hyper difficulty, which is basically this game's 'normal' difficulty - is that the difficulty balance between the stages and the bosses is very wide. Bosses are much more difficult, and the first three stages barely require effort to pass. It makes replays a little tedious. And you know this is bad when I'm coming from Touhou, which is infamous for boring first (and second, and sometimes third) stages. This game doesn't really get teeth until the final stage, other than the bosses. edit: Parallel difficulty fixes this by fixing the difficulty to the highest level. I really like this, actually. The difficulty curve is relatively flattened towards the upper end without the game having a level of difficulty requiring obsessive memorisation.

Talking of bosses, I really like that the final boss is a hard skill test. It mostly negates your bomb on use and prevents you from getting meter items, and while you can still pop it in a clutch moment for temporary self-invincibility, the boss actually gets more invincibility from using it than you do! While finishing a challenging shmup is always satisfying, bomb-spamming kills the impact of what should be the climax. The final boss itself is actually not particularly difficult, but because you're hard resource-capped its phases last longer and it turns into an extremely tense game of resilience, and scraping through that final phase and getting the win was intensely satisfying.

One small gripe is the poor feedback for the special. I find it difficult to tell when the special has been executed. There should be more audiovisual feedback. I'm using the piercing lancer and I can't even see the attack happening, and I'm often not sure that it has. This might vary depending on what special you use, and maybe if I used headphones there would be a discernible audio cue there?

Acción salvaje, suficientes opciones para regular la dificultad, armamento variado y nada de "farmeo" (sí, te miro a ti, SF).... el pixel art al principio me pareció un poco tosco: pero va a la perfección, como la música. La idea de "encadenar" series de disparos, y las mecánicas de puntuación aportan la suficiente novedad  mecánica, sin convertirse en un engorro ni ocultar lo importante: aquí has venido a moverte mucho por la pantalla y destrozar todo lo que se ponga por delante. Tal vez lo más desconcertante para mí sea que sólo tienes que evitar que las balas den a la cabina: una minúscula parte en el centro de tu nave. Así que, como ves en el trailer, puede haber miles de balas en pantalla... pero mientras tu cabina pase por el minúsculo espacio entre dos de ellas, estamos bien. Y eso de lanzar mi vehículo contra las balas se me hizo contraintuiivo. Pero nunca me quitó las ganas de continuar. Y sí, la cosa se pone infernal en muy poco tiempo, incluso en el nivel fácil... pero supongo que por eso en las opciones tienes un montón de opciones para personalizar aún más la dificultad. En resumen: un juego que rezuma atención al detalle y mimo en todos sus aspectos. Genial. Mi favorito en el género, con diferencia.

From the mind that later made Scrandle (small world I guess) is an excellent STG that taught me so much about the genre and I had a great time with. The game does a lot to hook you in, with the unlockables you can buy from the shop after every run and the mission mode teaching you basic ideas for score optimization, with lenient requirements to shoot for. The medals that show up for every weapon keeping track of if you completed the game or not with that weapon and in what difficulty prods you to try a variety of weapons. Stages 4 and 5 felt impossible to me at first without a defensive weapon, but after practicing a bunch using the game's stage select (also very accessible) and memorizing where the enemies will appear and how to lead bullets, they became 10x easier and a blast to play through every time. The flourish system is easy to understand and fun to plan out a route and take advantage of, and the break system is also great for getting you to move around the stage and keep track of what you're doing. In the end, though, the presentation is what I'll remember about the game. All the character designs are delightful and the stages look unique and perfect, especially stage 2. Music's also good, and them giving you three options for each song effectively means it'd be hard to get board of it. Very very easy to recommend.

Incredible shmup. I've cleared the game on Hyper difficulty without continues after about 17 hours of gameplay, so I like to think my two cents hold a bit of weight:

Game is very accessible thanks to settings such as "transparent player bullets" so you can focus on enemy fire, or you can also change the colours of enemy bullets if you have visibility problems. There's also a normal mode with autobombs, so people newer to the genre can give it a try too.

The scoring is very fun and allows for intricate, yet also surprisingly intuitive routing. Some other review said "it's DoDonPachi" which is pretty far from the truth. The chaining and usage of the flourish mechanic set Blue Revolver and DoDonPachi very far apart, and the same can be said for how resources work in this game. Even if you clip a bullet, if you have space for it in your "inventory", you get bombs back for scoring. As such, running into a bullet is a viable strategy sometimes. You'd never see that in DoDonPachi. Though, I will say that Mae's ship looks very similar to the one in DoDonPachi and her having a laser (if you decide so!) is pretty funny, but I see it as more of a "nod" than anything else. Blue Revolver has plenty of its own DNA, in fact it oozes of it.

The music is powerful and contributes to this game being an utter hype machine from the very start, but still building up that hype and the nerves as the run progresses. Even just a normal survival run gets very addicting that way.

I genuinely can't think of anything bad about this game, honestly. Worth full price, and if it's on sale and you love shmups, especially danmaku, this is a must try.

This my favorite SHMUP. There are many SHMUPs, but this one is for me.

Blue Revolver has a beautiful visual presentation with bright art style and detailed yet clean sprite work, great soundtrack (both original and DA remix). Three playable ships with different styles of shots and additionally multiple special weapons for each ship, enabling multiple play styles. Unlocks like screen filters and palettes, ship recolors, alternative music tracks. Many customization options.

But what really sold me on this game and got me hooked for dozens of hours is the scoring system. Basically, with regular shots you build a multiplier up, and then you can use special shots to "cash out" so to speak, making enemies killed by special weapons drop "coins" amount of which is dependent on your multiplier, and greatly increase your score. And certain special weapons may force you to adjust your playstyle to "cash out" and maximize your score. However you have a limited supply of special weapon ammo. And ammo sometimes drops from enemies, and also bomb kills always reward you special ammo. Certain score milestones give you tangible bonuses, for example reaching 5,000,000 gives you an extra life, which will certainly help you until you master the game enough to 1CC it (I'm still working on it). It's a very engaging scoring system that motivates you to be strategic, git gud and eventually compete for high scores. And a lot of challenge missions also utilize this scoring system with great success.

In addition to that, mini bosses and bosses have a Break mechanic, which basically gives you huge score bonuses for destroying certain parts of bosses in sequence or under certain conditions, (like for example, destroying small turrets before the main one). 

All this makes Blue Revolver Double Action's scoring very engaging and extremely satisfying to pull off.

There are many little things you could discover constantly replaying the game. Like for example sometimes you might want to sacrifice extra life on purpose, because respawning will refresh your bombs, and bomb kills drop ammo for your special weapons. But for that, you need to get extra lives by scoring high. You see where this is going?

All in all, it's a great SHMUP. As someone who was never big into nor good at them, this one finally clicked and made me understand the genre in general. And also became my favorite SHMUP.

I feel like it's time to finally write about this brilliant game. Sorry for the long review, but my rambling turned a bit passionate. From the early dev streams in 2015, the fun stage 1 community score attacks in early iterations, the v0.45 disc distributed at Touhoucon by woof that year (which came with a fantastic OST promotional minimix by Dyzphazia that I still listen to), to the eventual release in late 2016. While I wasn't keeping a keen eye on the game's development leading up to its release, when the game finally released its impact on the scene was large - marking what I believe was a pivotal point in the indie and doujin STG scene and contributing to the renaissance of the genre's future.

When Blue Revolver first came out, the game was like a breath of fresh air. Easy-to-grasp scoring mechanics, brutal rank-based difficulty, a killer aesthetic thanks to woof's art style and Qygen & Novaturtle's soundtrack. While the game did commit to a pixel style in-game, the flair of woof's artistry was preserved through the simplicity of the sprites and choice of colours, aiming to offer a seamless transition between the two mediums. The music offered a mix of electronic hardcore genres like techno and psytrance, high tempo and high BPM to match the high octane pacing of the gameplay. As an indie shoot 'em up, Blue Revolver offered one of the most complete packages of its kind.

The gameplay was everything you could expect from a bullet-hell STG: a large number of bullets, small player ship hitbox, evade and destroy them all to win the game. Easier said than done, of course. The game's scoring system is where the more intricate and technical aspect of the game lies. Destroy 8 ships (or objects) to max the hit counter, then cash it in by using your special shot to destroy things with a multiplier. Simple enough to understand so that new players wouldn't have to think too much when integrating it into their approach, but those seeking the elusive score extends may want to sit down and route out the optimal enemies to cash in on in the stage. The first set of extends are fairly obtainable without too much effort, with the score requirement subsequently increasing each time. The design isn't anything new but it offered a fun little taste for the lesser or uninitiated to try and push for more to increase their chances of survival. 

To make the scoring feel less stiff, the game introduced hidden "Break bonuses" throughout the run. They're a callback to a classic retro school of thought: If you perform some hidden requirement, you'll be offered bonus points. The number of Break bonuses in a stage are denoted by the Break counter at the end of a stage - with the exception Stage 5 which omitted the stage result screen (likely an intentional design to drive players like me insane on if we had found every Break). In similar fashion to the extends, the requirements for these hidden bonuses are usually lenient and new players will easily perform them on accident without any prior knowledge. This coupled with the Break counter in the stage result encouraged the player to try and approach sections differently and experiment, loosening the flow of the scoring system just enough so that they didn't feel completely anchored down when learning a level. 

The game was not without its flaws, however. Rank (dynamic difficulty) had always felt weird to me in the original iteration. In typical STG fashion, rank increases based on how well your perform/score and decreases when you die. While Normal and Parallel difficulty lock ranks at their respective values, Hyper took control of the full scale to provide a dynamic-feeling of difficulty. For me, I found that rank always raised faster than I could even hope to control it and often times I found myself wondering why I should even play Hyper when I usually found my rank in the realm of Parallel difficulty. To make things worse, certain sections of levels were designed a little too tightly to the core scoring system. This grew especially evident in the later stages where speedkilling would often result in "dead air" - an awkward state where you're waiting for 5-10 seconds with nothing to do until more enemies appear. At the time, I tolerated it, but as more indie/doujin STGs released, Blue Revolver unfortunately became the kind of game I could only recommend to genuine enthusiasts of the genre; there simply were better STGs out there. Blue Revolver walked so they could run.

danbo, the developer for Blue Revolver, was aware of the inherent problems in some of the game's flow. Perhaps "aware" is an understatement; true scrutiny of a work can only truly be done by its creator. If anyone was aware of its issues, it would be him.

Thus, Double Action was announced as a free arrange mode update, originally aiming to shift the gameplay of Blue Revolver and hopefully alleviate some of the problematic elements of its gameplay. To be included was a remixed soundtrack done by Exemia and Hagane. It sounded like it was going to breathe new life into the game.

But Double Action was delayed.

Forgive me ahead of time, I am far too lazy to do my research here and I didn't follow the development of Double Action too closely. I don't even recall when Double Action was announced other than it being what felt like ages ago, and soon my hype for it faded. The few glimpses I did see from danbo on twitter, however, made it clear that he was going through a rough patch in life. This was, in no doubt, exacerbated by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic which shook our world and changed a lot of how we lived our lives. I'll refrain from the digression, but the simple explanation was that many things were preventing danbo from fully realizing Double Action. To me, the arrange mode would release when it was ready.

Years went by and I completely forgot about the game. My life took a turn for a new career path and I was back in college in 2024 - when suddenly a public beta branch went up for Double Action, labeled as v1.50a (likely a reference to CAVE STGs having their infamous 1.5 rebalance). I played it for a run or two and really liked it, but my life was busy so that was as much as I played. Blue Revolver: Double Action released as a free update in November 2024 but I simply didn't have the time and completely forgot about it.

Nearly a year later, I finally sat down and put in some decent time into the game. What was previously envisioned as an arrange mode turned out to be a full game rebalance. Although the core scoring system remains the same, extends, rank values, special cash-in timings, and much more were adjusted to allow the game to be much more freeform. Additionally, some stage sections and bullet patterns were completely redone, with stage 5 feeling like a completely new game. Hyper difficulty no longer quickly ramps up to some pseudo-Parallel difficulty mode and extends. Normal and Hyper have extends every X-million points, which encourages an engaging gameplay loop. Score hard, intentionally die to have more resources to score harder and get even more lives. Parallel's difficulty retains the fixed extends but with a bomb awarded every 10-million points, cementing its identity as a difficulty where resources are plentiful but dying is a very real consequence.

Blue Revolver: Double Action became far more than just an arranged mode - it's the definitive version of the game to play. Double Action has pushed the game out of its pitfalls and secured itself alongside other shoot 'em ups in the hall of timeless masterpieces. Between the wonderfully vibrant visuals and choice of colours, it's robust, energetic, and pulsing soundtrack, and the rewarding scoring system amid its cut-throat gameplay, Blue Revolver has established an ageless identity for itself.

And to me, that is true success.
